title: Rudolph Levy, trumpet lessons with Fabian and the Arban method, health and age
summary: He mentions a former saxophonist's visit, the Arban method taught by Fabian, bronchitis and his habits and age.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: It might be a friend trying to get me. It might be a friend from out of town who wants to pay me a visit. My phone, as long as my wife was sick, no one knew my phone number. And one of my ex saxophonists who was part of my success came to town and the unionist had phone me first to ask me if I would let them give Rudolph Levy my phone number. I said, sure, give it to Rudolph. So I went to visit him. He stopped at the term mountain. We had chinchin for hours over. I don't know what his wife thought about him. He was his second wife. She's a nice woman too. He teaches bands now. He used to travel for the con company demonstrating the instruments. He was a clever man. The only man ever had to play a tune on a soprano saxophone. That is the B-A-S-T instrument, a soprano saxophone. It's so hard to play in tune on it, see? But he could play anything on tune. Some men are just natural born musicians. Ask me some more, sir. Yeah, about lessons. Who did I take from? Fabian. From Farley and Fabian. And how did he teach you? What did he do? He taught me from the Auburn method, which every trumpet player used, A-R-B-A-N, who was also a graduate and teacher at the Paris Conservatory of Music. My teacher was a first prize pupil from the Paris Conservatory, and he went back to France to help him out in World War I. And he died of something around with his bronchitis. I had bronchitis. They said I had chronic bronchitis just from that night work, playing trumpet, staying out all hours of night. But I'll say this, since I've retired, I don't have any more coughs, terrific coughs. But I used to see, I used to get fireworks displays, I used to suffer, cough, cough, cough, cough, cough. Now I don't, because I don't get up, I run from the wrong two-lane room out into the cold street to go over to the A&G to get a cup of coffee, because they wouldn't make you one, and you know, you're trying to, you know, try a thermos, the thing, but kind of a cheap guy. I never looked for favors anyhow, I never did. I'd go out of my way not to have to ask anything. If I asked a waiter to bring a man out of some ice water, he knew he could give a buck, give him a dollar. You've got to pay your way. And when I go in the blue room I'm a mock man, because they know me. The captain would come up and he'd say what did he do, did he take your order? He wants to give you five. Oh, I'd spend the five. I'd give it to the shoeshine boy. Like this, the suit. I went down to get a piece of some plywood cut to make this thing I'm going to make here. I have to use screws, they don't light a hammer in here, you don't use screws. So I drill a little hole with my drill number. I said to the man, he's an old man, but he's about my size. I said, you want this suit? He said, yeah. I said, well, wait till I get it off. I mean, my daughter says, get rid of it. So I'm the kind of a guy who doesn't like to see anything go to waste. These men who work in this place here tell you. The other day I gave them a thing that you put behind your hair when you wash your hair. I don't know how it got in the back of my car, they must have thrown everything in the back of the car. I gave away fishing tackle. I have plenty, I have too much. I'm a fellow that can't resist fishing tackle at the park. I've got to go in there and get something, buy something. It's a result that I have too much. And I had three bad vices, very bad. I like to fish, hunt and play golf. That's why I don't look 77, that's what they say. I don't know. But Mama lived to be 94. And I heard my lawyer, in the succession, they read something there that they think my lifespan will be 88. I don't know why that's in there, why is that in there? Well, if I left 88, I thank God right now. I'll try to be a good boy the rest of my life. And I have been a good boy.
